title: Building repertoire with fake books
summary: Blues, I Got Rhythm and practicing tunes.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: What do you advise a young player as far as building a jazz repertoire? Besides learning to play solos, are there certain tunes? Do you suggest these books, Fake Books?

Fake Books, yes, I do. And if you look through any of these books I was talking about, the jazz solos, the basic thing is you've got to learn the blues and variations of blues, the altered chords of the blues, "I Got Rhythm", "Honeysuckle Rose," the original names for dozens of later jazz pieces, "Undecided," "Just You, Just Me," that became a lot of jazz tunes, yeah, "Strike up the Band." Another jazz tune. There's 10 or 20 different jazz players with new melodies. And if you learn those basic tunes --

Now, most good jazz players, they don't just go out and hear the chords, which I myself thought a long time -- I have a good ear and I would not know a tune and I could still play it because I could anticipate what the next chord would be and even if I anticipated wrong, I could switch. And I could get through any tune. But I found out that good players, they practice tunes. You know, they don't leave it to chance, they take those tunes and turn them inside out, they run the chords, they run the scales and, you know, they don't just run them in root positions. Maybe in the beginning you have to run them in root positions but then you run them from the 3rd, you run them from the 5th, you run them from the 7th, and you run them the nearest note to the note you just left off, and you turn it every way, as they say, but loose. And then you can say you know the tune.
And then you go out and play and forget it. Just go
out and play. But then you can say you know the tune.
